clue.text: Position at end of battle after officer's retreat

indicators.note: the clue puts at and the battle's end after the officer, so they follow in the answer
to retreat is to go back, so the officer's abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: COL is the standard abbreviation for colonel, an army officer

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, here taken from battle

explanation.surface: A soldier takes up position once the fighting ends, after the commanding officer has pulled back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Position' reads as a military post, but it is a verb meaning to place or find.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to position something is to place or site it, as when you find where a thing belongs.

clue.text: Many turning tail never to be found

indicators.note: the tail of the word is its last pair of letters, and only those are turned round

parts.note: lots means many, a great number

explanation.surface: Plenty of people turn and run away, never to be seen again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning tail' swaps only the final two letters of LOTS, giving LOST.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something gone missing for good will never be found again.

clue.text: Episcopal staff from down under featured in Herald

indicators.note: something featured in another appears within it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a town crier is a herald, announcing news
Oz is the informal name for Australia, the land down under

explanation.surface: A bishop's staff from Australia gets a mention in a newspaper called the Herald.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herald' looks like a newspaper title but is the announcer; 'from down under' is the usual crossword pointer to Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a bishop carries a hooked pastoral staff as the badge of office, so it is an episcopal staff.

clue.text: Divine government chief welcomed by people in general

indicators.note: one welcomed by others is taken in among them, so a piece sits inside

parts.note: they, as in 'they say', means people in general
arch as a prefix means chief or principal, as in archbishop

explanation.surface: A leader with a godlike reign is received warmly by the public.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a rare word, from Greek for god plus rule; the wordplay builds it plainly.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition: rule by a god or gods, from Greek theos and archein, to rule; a rare word.

clue.text: Radical replacing agnostic's in charge, having an official staff

indicators.note: one thing replacing another takes its place, so the radical goes where in charge stood

parts.note: an agnostic is a sceptic, doubting God's existence
red means radical or left-wing in politics

explanation.surface: A radical takes over from an agnostic leader, now carrying an official rod of office.
explanation.walkthrough: In SCEPTIC, the IC is swapped for RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaning: a monarch's ornamental rod is the sceptre, so one holding it bears that staff, as in Shakespeare's 'sceptred isle'.

clue.text: Fireside repository of weird occult tales?

indicators.note: weird suggests the letters are strange and twisted out of place

explanation.surface: A spooky story-bin by the hearth holding eerie supernatural tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weird' shuffles OCCULT TALES. The hearthside box holds fuel, not stories; the question mark flags the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a metal bucket for fuel kept beside the hearth is a storage container at the fireside.

clue.text: Sound made by little dogs is irritating

indicators.note: the sound made by a word is how it is spoken, so the dogs are heard not seen

parts.note: pekes are Pekingese, small dogs

explanation.surface: The yapping of small dogs gets on your nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: PEKES (Pekingese dogs) is spoken the same as the answer, which is spelt the French way.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to pique someone is to annoy or nettle them, wounding their pride.

clue.text: Tenant clutching bottle's last to come in again

indicators.note: one clutching something holds it inside its grasp

parts.note: a renter is a tenant paying rent

indicators.note: the last of the word bottle is its final letter

explanation.surface: A tenant comes back into the flat holding the dregs of a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: E, the last letter of bottle, goes inside RENTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Formation: the prefix re- means again, so entering a second time is coming back in.

clue.text: Extremely desperate copyists giving marks out

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

parts.note: scribes copied manuscripts by hand

explanation.surface: Frantic copying clerks hand out grades on their work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes DE, the outer letters of desperate. 'marks' looks like grades, but means traces, as a compass traces a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometric sense: to trace a figure, as when a point traces a circle, is to mark out its shape.

clue.text: Second home of modest form, such as stoker uses

parts.note: a hovel is a humble, mean dwelling

explanation.surface: A second house, a humble one, of the sort a ship's stoker might have.
explanation.walkthrough: A stoker feeds a furnace or boiler with coal.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a stoker heaves coal into a furnace with a broad-bladed spade.

clue.text: Noble short crusade given God's protection

indicators.note: under the god's protection a thing is held within, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: Mars is the Roman god of war

indicators.note: short means cut, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a quest is a crusade or mission

explanation.surface: An aristocrat on a brief holy war is shielded by the Almighty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God' suggests the Christian deity of the crusade, but it is the Roman war god; 'given' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this title is a peer ranking above an earl and below a duke, so a nobleman.

clue.text: Wartime provision made by Disraeli — rather unorthodox

indicators.note: unorthodox means irregular, so the letters are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A wartime measure brought in by the Victorian prime minister in a rather odd way.
explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli was a 19th-century British prime minister, long before the Blitz, so the surface is pleasingly anachronistic.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: during the war bombing raids were met by refuges provided for civilians, as protection supplied by the authorities.

clue.text: Overlooking the very last pair, Nutmeg's almost useless

parts.note: the setter Nutmeg speaking of herself gives I'm, I am

indicators.note: overlooking means ignoring, so the final two letters are left off

parts.note: practically means almost, as in practically finished

explanation.surface: The setter, ignoring the final two items, admits she is nearly useless.
explanation.walkthrough: PRACTICALLY minus its last pair LY leaves PRACTICAL; Nutmeg is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Nutmeg's' is I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something unworkable or of no practical value is useless in real situations.

clue.text: Pious argument repelled all on aboard, you might say

indicators.note: repelled means driven back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a row is a quarrel or argument

parts.words: all on aboard, you might say
parts.note: a shipful would be everyone on board, a coinage the clue owns with 'you might say'

explanation.surface: A devout passenger's quarrel is pushed away by everyone on the boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repelled' turns ROW into WOR; 'you might say' admits SHIPFUL is a playful coinage for a full ship's company.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: devoted to worship, so reverent and devout; also an honorific for certain officials.

clue.text: Collaborators make worst bombs

indicators.note: a thing that bombs is blown apart, so the letters scatter into new places

explanation.surface: Accomplices produce the most terrible explosive devices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bombs' shuffles MAKE WORST. 'bombs' looks like a noun but works as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: colleagues who work side by side on the same job collaborate as a matter of course.

clue.text: Larva eats root

definitions.meaning: the soft wormlike young of an insect
slang for food, as in a plate of tasty eats
to dig or rummage about in soil, as a pig does

explanation.surface: An insect grub tucks into a plant's root.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions in a row: insect young, food, and to dig about.
explanation.definitionFit: Three senses: an insect's larval stage, informal food, and the verb of digging or rummaging.

clue.text: Protective paper

definitions.meaning: a newspaper, the British daily that publishes this very crossword

explanation.surface: A newspaper that looks after its readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: one who safeguards, used as a modifier, and the title of the British daily newspaper.

clue.text: River — harmful water source

parts.note: ill means harmful, as in ill effects

explanation.surface: A river described as a dangerous supply of drinking water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River' looks like the definition but supplies only R.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a tiny stream or brook, the sort of trickle that feeds a larger watercourse.

clue.text: Compared with acquaintance in song (foreign)

indicators.note: the acquaintance is placed in the song, so it goes inside

parts.note: Lied is the German word for a song, an art song
ken means knowledge or acquaintance, as in beyond one's ken

explanation.surface: A friend gets compared to someone in a foreign song.
explanation.walkthrough: '(foreign)' tells you the song word is German, the art song of Schubert and Schumann.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to say one thing resembles another is to compare the two.

clue.text: Decorative scrollwork details on limo

indicators.note: the details are placed on the limo, so they follow it

parts.note: a limo is a car
touches are small details or finishing strokes

explanation.surface: Ornamental curling trim fitted to a stretch limousine.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means placed after.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: oval ornamental frames or scroll-shaped tablets, as in architecture, or around Egyptian royal names in hieroglyphs.

clue.text: Ghastly appeal for sanctuary has nothing in it

indicators.note: the nothing goes in it, inside the appeal

parts.note: hide us is a plea to be given refuge
O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A dreadful plea for refuge turns out to have no substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has nothing in it' reads as emptiness but means a zero goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: extremely ugly or horrible to behold, as a ghastly sight is.

clue.text: Introduce trendy judge without filling court

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing

indicators.note: a word without its filling keeps only its outside letters

explanation.surface: Bring in a fashionable judge without packing the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without filling' empties judge to JE; 'filling court' looks like one phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to introduce a substance, or an idea, into something is to put or insert it.

clue.text: Finding success, mother and knight agreed to differ

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: letters made to differ are changed in their arrangement

explanation.surface: Mum and a knight reach a happy outcome by agreeing to disagree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agreed to differ' is a stock phrase, but here 'to differ' is the anagram signal alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to reach the required standard is to succeed, as students do in exams.

clue.text: Nonconformist church raised cross — what's the point?

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means turned upwards, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: URC is the United Reformed Church, a British Nonconformist denomination
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: A dissenting chapel puts up a cross, and someone asks why bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns URC (United Reformed Church, a British Protestant body outside the Church of England) into CRU.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the essential or central point of an issue, from Latin for cross.

clue.text: Leading couples refused to attend agency course

indicators.note: the first two letters of each word are refused, rejected and dropped

explanation.surface: The opening pairs turn down the chance to go on an agency training course.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the first two letters of each word: TO vanishes, ATTEND gives TEND and AGENCY gives ENCY.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a trend or inclination is the general course or drift that things follow.

clue.text: Very game old soldier returning punch

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: RU is rugby union, the game
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A spirited old trooper comes back to land a blow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns RU O GI into IGOUR. 'punch' is energy, not a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: punch is forcefulness or energy, as in a speech with real punch.

clue.text: Deliberately furtive about online meeting?

indicators.note: furtive goes about the meeting, wrapping round it

parts.note: sly means sneaky or furtive
an e-date is a date arranged or held online

explanation.surface: Someone is deliberately sneaky about a rendezvous arranged on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the online date is a coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: done calmly and unhurriedly, in a measured way, as something deliberate is.

clue.text: Colleges of yore catering for all

parts.note: unis is short for universities, colleges of higher learning
ex means former, of times past

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned universities that admitted everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catering for all' means suited to both sexes.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaning: designed for or suitable to both men and women, so catering for everyone alike.
